parole.significato: person or thing that does an action indicated by the root verb
parole.testo: From Danish -er, from Old Norse -ari, from Medieval Latin and Middle Low German words, both from Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz, from Latin -ārius.

parole.significato: An inflectional suffix forming the definite singular of neuter nouns, corresponding to English “the”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish -et (“neuter definite singular ending”), from Old Norse -it (“neuter definite singular ending”), the neuter form of the suffixed definite article. The modern pronunciation was influenced by native Norwegian developments in which the final consonant became silent. Compare Norweg

parole.significato: Used to form masculine nouns denoting the amount contained in, or the amount that fills, what the first element names.
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish -fuld (“noun-forming suffix denoting an amount that fills what the first element names”), from the suffixal use of fuld (“full”), ultimately from Old Norse fullr (“full”), from Proto-Germanic *fullaz (“full”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -full and English -ful (“noun-forming suff

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns, meaning full of, characterized by, showing, or possessing what the noun denotes; eq…
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish -fuld (“-ful; full of”), from the suffixal use of fuld (“full”), ultimately from Old Norse fullr (“full”), from Proto-Germanic *fullaz (“full”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -full, Danish -fuld, Swedish -full, Icelandic -fullur, Faroese -fullur, German -voll, Dutch -vol and Englis

parole.significato: A historical suffix forming nouns, originally chiefly abstract nouns, from nouns, adjectives, or other bases.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish -lig (“historical noun-forming suffix”), from Old Danish -lek (“noun-forming suffix”), corresponding to Old Norse -leikr (“play; form, appearance, nature”) and -leiki (“form, appearance, nature”); ultimately related to lek (“play, game”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -leik and Swed

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns, indicating that someone or something lacks, is without, or is free from what the no…
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish -løs (“-less; without, lacking”), ultimately from Old Norse -lauss (“-less; free from”), from Proto-Germanic *-lausaz (“loose, free”). The alternative -laus preserves the inherited Old Norse vowel. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -laus, Danish -løs, Swedish -lös, Icelandic -laus, Far

parole.significato: An inflectional suffix forming the synthetic passive infinitive and present tense of a verb.
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish -s (“verb ending”), from Old Norse -sk (“mediopassive ending”), formed through encliticization and contraction of sik (“oneself”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sek (“oneself”). Compare Swedish -s (“passive and deponent verb ending”), and Icelandic -st and Faroese -st (“middl

parole.significato: Used to form patronymics and patronymic surnames from male given names, meaning “son of”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish -sen, probably a reduced patronymic form of søn (“son”), from Old Norse sonr (“son”), from Proto-Germanic *sunuz (“son”). Corresponding to sønn (“son”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -sen and -son, Swedish -son, Icelandic -son and Faroese -son (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””)

parole.significato: expression of anger or sorrow, especially with a personal pronoun
parole.testo: Mostly likely from Norwegian ad (“against, on”), from Danish ad (“by, at”), from Old Danish at, from Old Norse at (“at, to”), from Proto-Germanic *at (“at, toward, to”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“to, at”).

parole.significato: an apple tree (any tree that bears apples, principally Malus domestica but also certain wild species)
parole.testo: From Danish abild (“European crab apple”), from Old Danish apæld, from Old Norse apaldr (“apple tree”), from Proto-Germanic *apaldraz (“apple tree”). Doublet of apal.

parole.significato: an apple blossom (the flower of an apple tree that will eventually turn into an apple)
parole.testo: abild + blomst, first part from Danish abild (“European crab apple”), from Old Danish apæld, from Old Norse apaldr (“apple tree”), from Proto-Germanic *apaldraz (“apple tree”). Last part from Danish blomst (“flower”), from the older blomster (“flower”), from Old Norse blómstr (“flower”), from Proto-

parole.significato: a branch of an apple tree
parole.testo: abild + gren, first part from Danish abild (“European crab apple”), from Old Danish apæld, from Old Norse apaldr (“apple tree”), from Proto-Germanic *apaldraz (“apple tree”). Last part from Danish gren (“branch, bough”), from Old Danish gren, from Old Norse grein (“branch, point, part”), from Proto-

parole.significato: white or light colour with gray spots; gray-spotted (of a horse)
parole.testo: abild + grå, first part from Danish abild (“European crab apple”), from Old Danish apæld, from Old Norse apaldr (“apple tree”), from Proto-Germanic *apaldraz (“apple tree”). Last part from Old Norse grár (“grey, spiteful”), from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz (“grey”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁- (“to

abild + gård, first part from Danish abild (“European crab apple”), from Old Danish apæld, from Old Norse apaldr (“apple tree”), from Proto-Germanic *apaldraz (“apple tree”). Last part from Danish gård (“farm, estate; court, yard”), from Old Danish garth, from Old Norse garðr (“fence; yard, court; h

parole.significato: an apple tree (any tree that bears apples, principally Malus domestica but also certain wild species)
parole.testo: abild + tre, from Danish abild (“European crab apple”), from Old Danish apæld, from Old Norse apaldr (“apple tree”), from Proto-Germanic *apaldraz (“apple tree”). Last part from Old Norse tré (“tree; beam”), from Proto-Germanic *trewą (“tree”), from pre-Germanic *dréwom, from Proto-Indo-European *dó

Probably a mixture of Danish abeløjer (“hijinks”), consisting of both abe (“monkey, ape”), from Old Norse api (“ape, monkey; fool”), from Proto-Germanic *apô (“ape, monkey”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep- (“(body of) water”) + løjer (“antics”), as well as Norwegian gøy (“fun”). Possibly f

parole.significato: night; an evening (the time of the day between dusk and night, when it gets dark)
parole.testo: From Danish aften (“evening; night”), from Old Danish aftæn, from Old Norse aptann (“evening”), from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþs (“evening”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi (“on, at, near”), of *h₁eps, of *h₁ep-. Cognate with Danish aften, Swedish afton, Faroese aftan and Icelandic aftann.
From Danish bager, from Old Norse bakari, from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz.
Inherited from Danish bede (pronounced /be/), from Old Norse biðja, from Proto-Germanic *bidjaną.

parole.significato: brook, creek, stream (body of running water smaller than a river)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish bæk, from Old Norse bekkr, from Proto-Germanic *bakiz, which see for cognates.
Inherited from Danish bælte, from Old Norse belti, from Proto-Germanic *baltiją, from Latin balteus.
From Danish ben, from Old Norse bein, from Proto-Germanic *bainą.
From Danish blæst, from Old Norse blástr. Doublet of blåst.

From Danish blomst (“flower”), from the older blomster (“flower”) (not to be confused with the modern indefinite plural form), from Old Norse blómstr (“flower”), from Proto-Germanic *blōmô (“flower”), from *blōaną (“to bloom, flower”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“to bloom, flower”). Cognate
From Danish bo, from Old Norse bú (“settled area, town”) (compare alternative form bu). Akin to bod (“store room, booth”) and the verb bo (“to live”).
From Danish bo, from Old Norse búa (“to prepare, finish, make preparations, equip”), cognate with Old English būan, Old Frisian buwa, Old Saxon būan and Old High German būan (whence German bauen).
Inherited from Danish bog with native Norwegian -k, from Old Norse bók (“book”), from Proto-Germanic *bōks (“letter”), which see. Often thought to be related with etymology 2 below.

From Danish borg, from Old Norse borg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“stronghold, city”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“fort”). Inherited with masculine declension from Danish, the optional feminine declension was later borrowed from Nynorsk.
From Danish brud, from Old Norse brot.

parole.significato: a landing stage, jetty, pier, wharf, dock (US)
parole.testo: From Danish brygge, from Old Norse bryggja.
From Danish brygge, from Old Norse *bryggva.

parole.significato: a coat of armour, particularly chain mail.
parole.testo: From Danish brynje, from Old Norse brynja (“coat of mail or plate”), from Proto-Germanic *brunjǭ (“breastplate”), possibly from Old Irish bruinne (“breast, bosom, chest”), from Proto-Celtic *brusnyos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to break”).

parole.significato: bread; a baked food made chiefly from flour and water, usually leavened with yeast or sourdough; also a loaf of this fo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish brød (“bread”), from Old Danish brøth, from Old Norse brauð (“bread”), from Proto-Germanic *braudą (“bread”). The deeper origin is disputed. Kroonen proposes a Proto-Indo-European pre-form *bʰrowh₁-tó-s, from the root *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil, seethe”), while another analysis regards

parole.significato: a well (hole sunk into the ground)
parole.testo: From Danish brønd, from Old Norse brunnr, from Proto-Germanic *brunnô (“source, wellspring, fountain”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrun- (“a bubbling forth; a fountain, wellspring, source”), from *bʰrew- (“to boil, brew”), from *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: a bow (used in archery and music)
parole.testo: From Danish bue, from Old Norse bogi, from Proto-Germanic *bugô.
From Danish bund, Old Danish botn, from Old Norse botn, from Proto-Germanic *butmaz. Doublet of botn.

parole.significato: town, city (regardless of population size or land area)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish by, from Old Norse býr (“place (to camp or settle), settlement”), derived from búa, whence bo.

Inherited from Danish byde, from Old Norse bjóða, from Proto-Germanic *beudaną (“to offer”). The contracted pronunciation is probably due to native Norwegian influence as it seems not to have been common in Danish (unlike other verbs such as bede, whence Bokmål be).
From Danish byrde, from Old Danish byrþi, byrthæ, from Old Norse byrðr.
From Danish båd, from Old Norse bátr, from Old English bāt (“boat”), from Proto-Germanic *baitaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd-.
Inherited from Danish bøg with native Norwegian -k, from Old Norse bók (“beech”), from Proto-Germanic *bōkō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos.
From Danish bønne, from Old Norse baun.
From Danish bøjle, from Old Norse bygill; compare with Norwegian Nynorsk bygel and German Bügel.
From Danish dam, from Old Norse dammr m, damm n. The meaning dam (structure) probably comes from Middle Low German [Term?].
From Danish davre, from Old Norse dagverðr, dǫgurðr. Doublet of dugurd.

Inherited from Danish deig, older spelling of dej, from Old Norse deig, from Proto-Germanic *daigaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead, form”). Compare Icelandic deig, Faroese deiggj, Swedish deg, English dough, Dutch deeg, German Teig. Further notes Mid-19th-century Danish retained an ot
From Danish digter from Old Norse diktari.
Inherited from Danish drage, from Old Norse draga, from Proto-Germanic *draganą. The contracted form is due to influence from Norwegian vernaculars. See English draw.

From Danish drikke, from Old Norse drekka (“to drink”), from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną (“to drink”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrenǵ- (“to draw into one's mouth, sip, gulp”), from *dʰreg- (“to draw, glide”). Cognates include English drink, German trinken, and Italian trincare.
From Danish drømme, from Old Norse dreyma (“to dream”), from Proto-Germanic *draumijaną. Cognate with English dream, Dutch dromen and German träumen.

parole.significato: economical, lasting, going a long way
parole.testo: From Danish drøj, from Old Norse drjúgr.

From Danish dyb, from Old Norse djúpr, from Proto-Germanic *deupaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb-. Cognates include Norwegian Nynorsk djup, Swedish djup, German tief, Dutch diep, English deep, and Gothic 𐌳𐌹𐌿𐍀𐍃 (diups).
Inherited from Danish dø, from Old Norse deyja, from Proto-Germanic *dawjaną (“to die”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk døy, Swedish dö, Icelandic deyja, English die.
Inherited from Danish død, from Old Norse dauði, dauðr (noun), from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz.
Inherited from Danish død, from Old Norse dauðr (adjective), from Proto-Germanic *daudaz.

parole.significato: the 24 hour period stretching from midnight to midnight.
parole.testo: From Danish døgn, from Old Norse dǿgn.
From Danish døbe, from Old Norse deypa.
From Danish døv, from Old Norse daufr, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-.
Inherited from Danish æble, from Old Norse epli.
From Danish eventyr, from late Old Norse æfintýr, from Middle Low German eventü̂r, from Middle French adventure (“aventure”).
From Danish evne, from Old Norse efni. Cognate with Swedish ämne (“subject”), doublet of emne (“subject”).

From Danish falde (pre-1907 spelling in Riksmål), from Old Norse falla (“to fall”), from Proto-Germanic *fallaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pōl-. Cognates include Faeroese and Swedish falla, Danish falde, English fall, German fallen.
Inherited from Danish femten, from Old Norse fimmtán, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun.
Inherited from Danish færge, from Old Norse ferja, from Proto-Germanic *farjǭ (noun) and *farjaną (“verb”).

From Danish finde, from Old Norse finna, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass; path, bridge”). Cognates include Danish finde, Swedish finna, Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌽𐌸𐌰𐌽 (finþan), German finden, Dutch vinden, and English find.
Inherited from Danish fire, from Old Norse fjórir, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr, which see.
Inherited from Danish fjorten, from Old Norse fjórtán, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun.

Inherited from Danish flod, from Old Norse flóð, from Proto-Germanic *flōduz. Doublet of flod (“flood, river”). The last-mentioned senses, perhaps due to their biblical and literary associations, predominantly have a more spelling-based pronunciation in /d/ not common for the sense “high tide”. This

Inherited from Danish flod, from Old Norse flóð (“flood”), from Proto-Germanic *flōduz. Doublet of flo (“high tide”). The Danish word (like Swedish flod) acquired the sense “river” through influence of Middle Low German vlôt f, from the same etymon as above, as well as related vlȫt(e) m, from Proto-
From Danish flue, from Old Norse fluga f, from Proto-Germanic *flugǭ. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk fluge, flugu (dialectal flue).
Inherited from Danish folk, from Old Norse fólk, folk, from Proto-Germanic *fulką.
Inherited from Danish frem, from Old Danish fræm, an alteration (by analogy with the comparative and superlative forms) of older fram, from Old Norse fram.
From Danish frænde, from Old Norse frændi.
From Danish fryd, from Old Norse frygð (“magnificence, splendour”); cognate with Old High German frewida, German Freude, and Icelandic frygð.
Inherited from Danish fugl, from Old Norse fugl, fogl, from Proto-Germanic *fuglaz.

From Danish fuld, from Old Norse fullr, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós. Cognates include Swedish full, Norwegian Nynorsk full, Icelandic fullur, German voll, Dutch vol, English full, Gothic 𐍆𐌿𐌻𐌻𐍃 (fulls), Lithuanian pilnas, Old Church Slavonic плънъ (plŭnŭ), Latin pl
Inherited from Danish få, from Old Norse fár. Cognates include English fang, German fangen, and German vangen.

parole.significato: to get; to have; to obtain; to receive.
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish få, from Old Norse fá (to grab, capture, conquer), from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną.
From Danish følge, from Old Norse fylgja.

parole.significato: old (of an object, concept, etc: having existed for a relatively long period of time)
parole.testo: From Danish gammel, from Old Norse gamall, compare native gammal; comparative and superlative forms from Old Norse ellri and Old Norse ellztr.

parole.significato: to give (to transfer the possession of something to someone else)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish give, from Old Danish gifæ, from Old Norse gefa, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-.
From older Danish giftermaal (modern Danish giftermål), from Old Norse giptarmál.
From Danish gidsel, from Old Norse gísl, from Proto-Germanic *gīslaz.

parole.significato: through (from one side of an opening to the other)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish gjennem, older spelling of gennem, from Old Norse gegnum, dative plural of gegn. The spelling in -om was influenced by Nynorsk. Gjennom and mellom (“between”) were introduced as byforms in Bokmål in 1917 and made the sole standard in 1938. Though rare up until that time, they e
From Danish gøg (older spelling gjøg), from Old Norse gaukr.

The plural is inherited from Danish gløder with a contracted pronunciation comparable to klær, spar. The singular appears to be of dialectal Norwegian origin. Doublet of glød (“glow, heat”). All further from Old Norse glóð, from Proto-Germanic *glōdiz (“ember, red heat”).

Inherited from Danish glo (“to stare”, archaic “to glow”), from Old Norse glóa, from Proto-Germanic *glōaną (“to glow”), related with etymology 1 above. The semantic development perhaps from the idea of “glowing eyes”.

parole.significato: red heat, the state of glowing (as of an ember)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish glød, from Old Norse glóð, from Proto-Germanic *glōdiz. Doublet of glo (“ember”).

parole.significato: spruce (mostly the species Picea abies (Norway spruce)).
parole.testo: From Danish gran, from Old Norse grǫn (“spruce, pine tree”), from Proto-Germanic *granō (“awn, bristles”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰroH-néh₂-.
From Danish gren (“branch, bough”), from Old Danish gren, from Old Norse grein (“branch, point, part”), from Proto-Germanic *grain-.
From Danish grib, from Old Danish gryp, from Old Norse gripr (“vulture, griffin”), from Latin gryps, probably via Middle Low German grip. Compare Old Irish gríb (“gyrfalcon, griffin”).

From Danish gribe (“to grab”), from Old Norse grípa (“to grab”), from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grasp, grab”). Cognate with Danish gribe, Swedish gripa, Icelandic grípa, English gripe, Dutch grijpen, German greifen.
From Danish gud, from Old Norse goð, guð, from Proto-Germanic *gudą.
From Danish guld (pre-1907 Riksmål spelling), from Old Norse gull, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą.

From Danish gård (“farm, estate; court, yard”), from Old Danish garth, from Old Norse garðr (“fence; yard, court; house”), from Proto-Germanic *gardaz (“enclosure, court, yard, garden”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos, from *gʰerdʰ- (“to enclose, encircle”).
From Danish halm, from Old Norse halmr.

From Danish havn, from Old Norse hǫfn (“port, harbor, haven”), from Proto-Germanic *habanō, *habnō (“harbour, haven”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂póneh₂ or *kh₂pnéh₂, from the root *kap- (“to take, seize, grasp”).
From Danish hellig, from Old Danish hælægh, like Old Norse heilagr (Norwegian Nynorsk heilag) from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz.

From Danish hest, from Old Danish hæst (“horse”), from Old Norse hestr (“horse”), from Proto-Germanic *hangistaz (“horse, stallion”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱanḱest-, *kankest- (“horse”). Doublet of hingst.

parole.significato: An informal retinue of personal armed companions.
parole.testo: From Danish hird, from Old Norse hirð, a borrowing from Old English hīred, from Proto-West Germanic *hīwarād.

From Danish hjem, from Old Danish hēm, hiem, from Old Norse heimr, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home, house”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos (“village, home”), *tḱóymos (“settlement, dwelling”), from o-grade form of *tḱey- (“to settle, dwell”) + *-mos (action/result noun forming suffix).
From Danish hjemme (“at home, home”), from Old Danish hemæ, hemmæ, from Old Norse heima. Also cognate with Old Saxon hēme and Old High German heime (“at home”).
From Danish hjemmel and Old Danish hemæl, from Old Norse heimild.
From Danish hjord, from Old Norse hjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *herdō, cognate with Danish, Swedish hjord, English herd, German Herde.

From Danish hoved, from Old Danish houæth, from Old Norse hǫfuð, from Proto-Germanic *hafudą, *habudą, northern form of *haubudą, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *kaput- (“head”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk hovud, Swedish huvud, Icelandic höfuð, English head, Dutch hoofd, German Haupt. The fo
Inherited from Danish holde, from Old Norse halda, from Proto-Germanic *haldaną. See English hold.
Inherited from Danish hoste, from Old Norse hósti, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstô
Inherited from Danish hoste, from Old Norse hósta (sense 1), and English host (sense 2). The Old Norse verb is from Proto-Germanic *hwōstōną
From Danish hun, from Old Norse hón.

Inherited from Danish hvad, from Old Norse hvat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. The loss of the final consonant is also common in Danish, but was reinforced by native Norwegian dialects; cf. Nynorsk kva and eastern dialect forms such as (h)å.
From Danish hval, from Old Norse hvalr, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”).
From Danish hvem, from Old Norse hveim. Known in a runic spelling as huem (with a bind rune) in a magical manuscript from around 1650.

From Danish hverdag. Compound of hver (“every”) + dag (“day”), from Old Norse hverr (“every”) dagr (“day”). Semantic shift of uncertain origin. Probably, from the original meaning "every day which is not a holy day". Plausibly under the influence of similar-sounding German "Werktag".

parole.significato: hverken … eller – neither … nor, (after a negative) either … or
parole.testo: From Danish hverken, from Old Norse hvárgi.
From Danish hvede, from Old Norse hveiti, from Proto-Germanic *hwaitijaz, from *hwītaz (“white”).
Inherited from Danish hvid with -t under influence of native Norwegian kvit, both from Old Norse hvítr, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweytos.

parole.significato: arctic hare (Lepus arcticus); a species of hare native to Arctic regions of northern Canada and Greenland, especially s…
parole.testo: hvit (“white”) + hare (“hare”), literally “white hare”. The first element, hvit (“white”), continues Danish Inherited from Danish hvid (“white”), with final -t under the influence of native Norwegian kvit (“white”); ultimately from Old Norse hvítr (“white”), from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz (“white”), ul
From Danish hvor, from Old Norse hvar.

parole.significato: flax (a plant of the genus Linum, especially Linum usitatissimum, as well as its fibers)
parole.testo: From Danish hør, from Old Norse hǫrr (“linen”), from Proto-Germanic *hazwaz (“flax, linen”), of unknown origin.
From Danish høre, from Old Norse heyra, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti.
Inherited from Danish ihjel, from Old Norse í hel. Compare to Swedish ihjäl and Norwegian Nynorsk i hel.
From Danish idræt, from Old Danish idræt, from Old Norse íþrótt.
From Danish ikke, from Old Norse ekki (“not”). Cognate with Swedish icke, Norwegian Nynorsk ikkje, Faroese ikki, and Icelandic ekki.
From Danish isse, from Old Danish jassæ, jæssæ, jessæ, issæ, all from Old Norse hjarsi, hjassi, from Proto-Germanic *hersô. Cognates include Swedish hjässa and Norwegian Nynorsk hjasse.
From Danish jatte, jætte, from Old Danish jate, from Old Norse játa, játta, from Proto-Germanic *jaatjaną.
From Danish jeg, from Old Norse ek (Old East Norse jek). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm.
From Danish jord, from Old Norse jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er-. Compare to Nynorsk jord.
From Danish kar, from Old Norse ker, in the sense of blood vessels influenced by Latin vas.

parole.significato: a core, pit, seed (the central part of a fruit, containing the kernels or seeds)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish kjerne, kjærne, older spelling of kerne (“core”), from Old Norse kjarni, from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“core, kernel”), which see.

parole.significato: a churn (a vessel used for churning, especially for producing butter)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish kjerne, kjærne, older spelling of kærne (“churn”), from Old Norse kirna, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ.

parole.significato: to churn (agitate rapidly and repetitively, or stir with a rowing or rocking motion, specifically to create butter)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish kjerne, kjærne, older spelling of kærne (“to churn”), from Old Norse kirna, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijaną, closely related with etymology 2 above.
Inherited from Danish kjær, older spelling of kær, from Old Norse kærr, which see.

Verbal noun form of kjøpe (“to buy, purchase”), from Danish købe (“to buy, purchase”), from Old Danish køpæ (“to buy, purchase”), from Old Norse kaupa (“to buy, purchase”), from Proto-Germanic *kaupaz (noun), from Latin caupō (“tradesman, innkeeper, shopkeeper, tavern-keeper”).

From Danish købe (“to buy, purchase”), from Old Danish køpæ (“to buy, purchase”), from Old Norse kaupa (“to buy, purchase”), from Proto-Germanic *kaupaz (noun), from Latin caupō (“tradesman, innkeeper, shopkeeper, tavern-keeper”).
Inherited from Danish klæde (pronounced /klɛ/), from Old Norse klæða.
Inherited from Danish klæde, from Old Norse klæði, borrowed from a descendant of Proto-West Germanic *klaiþ.
Inherited from Danish klø, from Old Norse kleyja. Related with klo and klå. The form kleie is from the Old Norse variant klæja, corresponding to obsolete Danish kle.
Inherited from Danish kvæde, from Old Norse kveða, from Proto-Germanic *kweþaną (“to say”).

parole.significato: a chick (young of a domestic fowl)
parole.testo: From Danish kylling, from Old Danish kykling, from Old Norse kjúklingr.

parole.significato: to rent, hire (use or borrow for payment)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish leje, from Old Norse leiga, from Proto-Germanic *laigijaną.

parole.significato: rental, rent (agreement that something can be used or borrowed for payment)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish leje, from Old Norse leiga, from Proto-Germanic *laigǭ. Closely related with etymology 1 above.

parole.significato: the act of lying (down), a certain way thereof
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish leje, from Old Norse lægi, from Proto-Germanic *lēgiją. Compare prefixed Middle High German gelæge (German Gelege).

parole.significato: a lot (that is cast or drawn)
parole.testo: From Danish lod and Old Norse hlutr (senses 1-2) and Middle Low German lot (senses 3-6).
From Danish lov (“law”), of Old Danish logh (“law”), from Old Norse lǫg (“law”), plural of lag (“layer”), from Proto-Germanic *lagą (“situation, law”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”).
From Danish lyd, from Old Norse hljóð (“a sound”).

parole.significato: to sound (produce a sound), to be heard
parole.testo: From Danish lyde, from Old Danish lythæ, from Old Norse hljóða (“sound”).

parole.significato: to obey (do as one is told)
parole.testo: From Danish lyde, from Old Norse hlýða (“obey”).
From Danish lys, from Old Norse ljóss, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsaz.
From Danish lys, from Old Danish liūs, from Old Norse ljós, Proto-Germanic *leuhsą.
Inherited from Danish lyve, from Old Norse ljúga, from Proto-Germanic *leuganą.
Inherited from Danish lår, from Old Norse *lār ~ lær, from Proto-Germanic *lahwaz (z-stem).
Inherited from Danish løbe with native Norwegian -p-, from Old Norse hlaupa, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną. Cognates include English leap; see the Proto-Germanic for more.
Inherited from Danish lørdag, from Old Norse laugardagr (“bath day”).
From Danish løf, from Old Norse lauf, from Proto-Germanic *laubą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewp- (“peel, break off”). Cognate with English leaf.

From Danish mandag, from Old Norse mánadagr, from late Proto-West Germanic *mānini dag, a calque of Latin dies lunae. Compare Danish mandag, Swedish and Norwegian Nynorsk måndag, Icelandic mánudagur, Faroese mánadagur.

From Danish mand (pre-1907 Riksmål spelling), from Old Norse mann, accusative case of maðr (“man”) (compare the accusative of Icelandic maður). Originally the word only had the sense "human" but later changed to primarily designate an adult male, the original meaning being replaced by words such as
From Danish mel, from Old Norse mjǫl.

parole.significato: milk (nutritious liquid produced by a lactating mammalian mother)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish mælk, from Old Norse mjolk, mjǫlk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-. Compare with Danish mælk, Swedish mjölk, Icelandic mjólk.

parole.significato: between (X and Y, i.e., mellom X og Y)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish mellem, from Old Norse í millum, plural variant of Old Norse í milli (“in the middle”). The spelling in -om was influenced by Nynorsk; see gjennom (“through”) for more.
From Danish mens, from older medens, from Old Norse meðan.

parole.significato: morning (the part of the day when the night ends and the day begins, dawn)
parole.testo: From Danish morgen, from Old Norse morginn, morgunn, from Proto-Germanic *murganaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥Hko (“to blink, twinkle”). Compare Swedish morgon, Icelandic morgunn, English morn, morrow, Dutch morgen, German Morgen.
From Danish mund (pre-1907 Riksmål spelling), from Old Norse muðr, munnr, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *men-.

From Danish måned (“month”), from Old Danish maanædh, from Old Norse mánuðr, mónuðr, mánaðr (“month”), from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþs (“month”), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”), from earlier *méh₁n̥ss, from *meh₁- (“to measure”). Doublet of måne.
Inherited from Danish måtte, from Old Norse mega, from Proto-Germanic *maganą. The modern infinitive was backformed from the past tense (Old Norse mátta) by analogy with kunne, skulle, ville.
From Danish nabo, from Old Norse nábúi.
From Danish narhval. Probably by metathesis from Old Norse náhvalr "corpse whale", based on nár (“corpse”) and hvalr (“whale”).
Inherited from Danish negl, from Old Norse nagl (“nail”), from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-.

parole.significato: a headland (coastal land that juts into the sea)
parole.testo: From Danish næs, from Old Norse nes (“headland”), from Proto-Germanic *nasją (“foothill; headland, cape”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s (“nose”). Cognate with Faroese nes, Icelandic nes, Danish næs and possibly Norman nez.
From Danish nord, from Old Norse norðr, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą.
Inherited from Danish nå, from Old Norse ná, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwijaną.
From Danish nød, from Old Norse nauð, nauðr, from Proto-Germanic *naudiz, *nauþiz.
Inherited from Danish nød with native Norwegian -t, from Old Norse hnot, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts.
From Danish ost, from Old Norse ostr.
From Danish pige, from Old Norse píka.
From Danish ploug, older spelling of plov, from Old Norse plógr. The pronunciation is based on native Norwegian dialects.
From Danish pose, from Old Norse posi.
From Danish ravn, from Old Norse hrafn, from Proto-Germanic *hrabnaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-.

parole.significato: hall (large room in which parties, meetings etc. are held)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish sal, from Old Norse salr, from Proto-Germanic *salą.
Inherited from Danish salg, from older sal, from Old Norse sal (“payment”).
From Danish savn, derived from savne, from Old Norse sakna (“to miss”).
From Danish se, from Old Norse sjá, from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną. Cognates include English see and Dutch zien.
From Danish sejr (“victory”), from Old Norse sigr (“victory”), from Proto-Germanic *segaz.
From Danish seig, older spelling of sej, from Old Norse seigr. The alternative spoken form with a pronounced [ɡ] is influenced by Norwegian dialects.

parole.significato: sail (piece of fabric attached to a boat’s mast)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish seil, older spelling of sejl, from Old Norse segl, from Proto-Germanic *seglą.

parole.significato: to sail (travel in a boat or ship, especially by sail)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish seile, older spelling of sejle, from Old Norse sigla, from Proto-Germanic *siglijaną.

parole.significato: to be triumphant or victorious, to conquer, win
parole.testo: From Danish sejre, from Old Norse sigra.
Inherited from Danish seksten, from Old Norse sextán, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun.

parole.significato: to sell (agree to transfer goods or provide services in return for payment)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish sælge, from Old Norse selja (“to sell”), from Proto-Germanic *saljaną.

Inherited from Danish sælger, from Old Norse seljari. By surface analysis, selge (“to sell”) + -er. While ⟨g⟩ is always silent in the verb, compare salg (“sale”) with /ɡ/. The words selger and selgelig (“vendible”, now more usually salgbar) vary between both ways.
From Danish selv, from Old Norse sjalfr, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”), from *s(w)e- (“separate, apart”).

From Danish sænke, from Old Danish sænckæ, from Old Norse *sænkja (east) / søkkva (west), from Proto-Germanic *sankwijaną, cognate with German senken. Causative of Proto-Germanic *sinkwaną (“to sink”) (cf. Danish synke (“to sink”)).

Inherited from Danish sæde with native Norwegian -t-, from Old Norse sæti, from Proto-Germanic *sētiją. Cognate with Swedish säte, and (with prefix) German Gesäß, Middle Low German gesête, Middle Dutch gesâte.
From Danish siden, compare the Norwegian-derived sia, from Old Norse síðan. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk sidan and Swedish sen.
From Danish sild, from Old Norse sild, síld.
From Danish skæv (skjæv, skjev), from Old Danish skev, from Old Norse skeifr.

parole.significato: a shield (used as protection in battle)
parole.testo: From Danish skjold, from Old Danish skiold, from Old Norse skjǫldr m, from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keit-, *(s)keid-, *kheit- (“shield, cover”). Compare with Danish skjold, Swedish sköld, Icelandic skjöldur.

parole.significato: To cut with a knife or a similar tool, to slice
parole.testo: From Danish skære, from Old Norse skera (“to cut”), from Proto-Germanic *skeraną (“to shear”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Cognate with Danish skære, Swedish skära, Faroese and Icelandic skera, Old English scieran, English shear, and Dutch and German scheren.
From Danish skyde, from Old Norse skjóta, from Proto-Germanic *skeutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd-.
From Danish slange, from Old Norse slangi. Also from Middle Low German slange.

parole.significato: to extinguish, put out (e.g. a fire)
parole.testo: From Danish slukke, from Old Norse sløkkva.
From Danish smør, from Old Norse smjǫr, smør, from Proto-Germanic *smerwą. See also the verb smøre. Cognate with English smear.
Inherited from Danish smøre, from Old Norse smyrja. See also the noun smør. Cognate with English smear.
Inherited from Danish snegl, from Old Norse snigill, from Proto-Germanic *snigilaz. The form in -e was backformed from the inflected forms, likely under influence of the Norwegian variant snile.
From Danish snige, from Old Norse sníkja, from Proto-Germanic *snīkaną. More at sneak.
From Danish sort, from Old Danish sort, swort, swart, from Old Norse svartr, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swordo- (“dirty, dark, black”).
From Danish spyd, from Old Danish spiut, from Old Norse spjót, from Proto-Germanic *speutą.
From Danish stabel, Old Norse stǫpull and Middle Low German stapel; compare with German Stapel. Doublet of støpul.

From Danish stad, from Old Danish stath, from Old Norse staðr (“place, spot, city, town”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“place, location”), from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis (“standing, position”), from *steh₂- (“to stand (up)”) + *-tis (“derives abstract/action nouns from verb roots”).
From Danish stavn, in turn from Old Norse stafn.
From Danish sted, from Old Danish stath, stæth, from Old Norse staðr m.
Inherited from Danish stjæle, from Old Danish stiælæ, from Old Norse stela, from Proto-Germanic *stelaną.
From Danish stol, from Old Norse stóll, from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *stāl- (“frame, rack, stand”).
From Danish strøm, from Old Norse straumr, from Proto-Germanic *straumaz, from Proto-Indo-European *srowmos, from *srew- (“to flow”).
From Danish stue, from Old Norse stofa, stufa, borrowed from Middle Low German stōve, stūve, Old Saxon *stova, *stuva, from Proto-West Germanic *stobu.
Inherited from Danish syd, from Old Norse syðri.
Inherited from Danish syd, from Old Norse suðr.
Inherited from Danish syg with consonantal influence by native Norwegian sjuk, both from Old Norse sjúkr, from Proto-Germanic *seukaz.
From Danish syvende, from Old Norse sjaundi.
From Danish søndag, from Old Norse sunnudagr, from Proto-West Germanic *sunnōn dag, a calque of Latin dies Solis.
From Danish sørge, from Old Danish sørghiæ, syrghia, from Old Norse syrgja.

From informal Danish taknemlig (the standard Danish spelling was taknemmelig, now both are standard, but not in Norwegian), from Old Danish taknem with suffix -lig, probably influenced by Old Norse þakknæmiligr and Middle Low German danknamelik. Compare Swedish tacknämlig.

Inherited from Danish toug (now spelt tov), from Old Norse tog, from Proto-Germanic *tugą. The unusual spelling ⟨oug⟩ was pronounced according to dialectal Norwegian (as in baug, plog). Underlying dialectal forms continue the Old Norse ablaut variant taug, from Proto-Germanic *taugō. Standardized as
Inherited from Danish tegn, from Old Norse teikn, from Proto-Germanic *taikną (“sign, token”).
Inherited from Danish t(h)egn, from Old Norse þegn, from Proto-Germanic *þegnaz.
From Danish tælle, from Old Norse telja, from Proto-Germanic *taljaną.
From Danish tirsdag, from Old Norse týsdagr, týrsdagr, from Týr (“Tyr”) and dagr (“day”), from Proto-West Germanic *Tīwas dag, a calque of Latin dies Martis.
From Danish tjeneste, from Old Norse þjónusta, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz.

Inherited from Danish trænge, from Old Norse þrøngva, from Proto-Germanic *þrangwijaną (“to press, to push”). In some uses the Danish verb probably absorbed the related strong verb Old Norse þryngva, from Proto-Germanic *þrinhwaną.
Inherited from Danish træt, from Old Norse þreyttr.
Inherited from Danish tretten, from Old Norse þrettán, from Proto-Germanic *þritehun.
From Danish tyr, from Old Norse þjórr, from Proto-Germanic *þeuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros, whence also Latin taurus, Ancient Greek ταῦρος (taûros), Old Irish tarb.
From Danish tyv, from Old Norse þjófr, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz.
From Danish uge, from Old Norse vika, from Proto-Germanic *wikǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, wind, turn, yield”).

From Danish urt, from Old Norse urt, from Proto-Germanic *wurtiz, cognate with Swedish ört, English wort. A variant of *wrōts (“root”) (Norwegian Bokmål rot). The form urta is from oral Norwegian (see Norwegian Nynorsk urta).
Inherited from Danish vanlig, from Old Norse vanaligr. Compare Swedish vanlig, Icelandic vanalegur and Norwegian Nynorsk vanleg.

parole.significato: water; the chemical compound H₂O, especially as a clear, colourless and odourless liquid
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish vand (“water”), from Old Danish watn (“water”), also attested as wadn and wand, corresponding to Old Norse vatn (“water”), from Proto-Germanic *watōr (“water”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”), from the root *wed- (“water; wet”). The alternative form vatn (
From Danish vante, from Old Norse vantr.

Inherited from Danish vaske, from Old Norse vaska (“to wash”), from Proto-Germanic *waskaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wod- (“wet; water”). Cognate with Swedish vaska, German waschen, Old English wæscan (English wash). The simple past tense is from oral Norwegian (compare to the declensio
Inherited from Danish vej, from Old Norse vegr, from Proto-Germanic *wegaz.
From Danish vælge, from Old Norse velja. See German wählen.

From Danish verden, from Old Danish werdhen, originally singular definite form of wæræld, wærild, wærælde, from Old Norse verǫld, whence verd, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz. The original indefinite form was rarely used so much so the definite form was interpreted as the indefinite form, hence the et
Inherited from Danish vest, from Old Norse vestr, from Proto-Germanic *westrą.

parole.significato: to want to, be willing to
parole.testo: From Danish ville, from Old Norse vilja, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-.
From Danish vind, from Old Norse vindr, from Proto-Germanic *windaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts (“blowing”), present participle of *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

Inherited from Danish vindue, from Old Norse vindauga. The final -e is already largely silent in Danish. In Norway, this pronunciation may have been reinforced by backformation from the definite form.
From Danish voks, from Old Danish wax, wox, from Old Norse vax, from Proto-Germanic *wahsą.
From Danish vokse, from Old Norse vaxa.
From Danish vride and Old Danish writhæ, from Old Norse ríða, vríða.
From Danish vågen, from Old Norse vakinn, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be strong”). This form, as opposed to vaken, is due to influence from Danish vågen.

parole.significato: a weapon; arms (an instrument of attack or defense in combat or hunting, e.g. most guns, missiles, or swords)
parole.testo: From Danish vaaben, from Old Norse vápn (“weapon”), from Proto-Germanic *wēpną (“weapon”). Cognate with Swedish vapen, Dutch wapen, German Wappen and English weapon.

Inherited from Danish vejr, from Old Norse veðr, from Proto-Germanic *wedrą (“weather”), which see for cognates and further origin. The Danish word is generally pronounced /vɛːr/ and an according spelling vær was found in older Danish. Native Norwegian dialects (cf. Nynorsk vêr) coincide.

Inherited from Danish væder, older spelling of vædder (whence now displaced Bokmål vedder), from Old Norse veðr, from Proto-Germanic *weþruz (“male sheep”), which see. The contracted form vær is comparable to lær, klær, as well as vær (etymology 1 above). Native Norwegian influence (cf. Nynorsk vêr)

All forms except the present are from Danish være, from Old Norse vera, from Proto-Germanic *wesaną (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes- (“to dwell, live, reside”). The present tense is derived from a different root: Proto-Germanic *izum, *izud, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be”), whic
Inherited from Danish ydmyge, from Old Norse auðmýkja.
Probably from Danish ånd, which in turn comes from Old Norse ǫnd, a variant of andi.

From Danish ånde (“breath”), from Old Danish andæ, from Old Norse andi (“breath; spirit, soul”), from Proto-Germanic *anadô (“breath; spirit, zeal”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁-dʰō, from *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”), likely of onomatopoeic origin.

From Danish aaben, from Old Norse opinn, from Proto-Germanic *upanaz, from Proto-Indo-European *up. Compare with Icelandic opinn, Swedish öppen, Dutch open, Low German apen, open, German offen, West Frisian iepen, English open.

From Danish øl, from Old Norse ǫl, from Proto-Germanic *alu, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elut- (“beer”). The short-vowel pronunciation was originally chiefly restricted to Oslo, for which reason the form øl, ølet was standardized instead of øll, øllet (cf. Danish øl, øllet). However, this pronunciat
From Danish øre, from Old Danish øræ, from Old Norse eyra, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic *ausô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ous-.
From Danish ørred, from Old Norse aurriði.
From Danish øst, from Old Norse austr.

From Danish øje, replaced native aue, from Old Danish øghæ, from Old Norse auga, from Proto-Germanic *augô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk auga, auge, Icelandic auga, Faroese eyga and Swedish öga.
